A.actClause: AN ACT to amend the not-for-profit corporation law, the religious corporations law, the estates, powers and trusts law, the surrogate's court procedure act and the executive law, in relation to adopting a prudent management of institutional funds standard; and to repeal certain provisions of the not-for-profit corporation law relating thereto
A.memo:
BILL NUMBER:A7907A

TITLE  OF  BILL:   An act to amend the not-for-profit corporation law,
the religious corporations law, the estates, powers  and  trusts  law,
the surrogate's court procedure act and the executive law, in relation
to  adopting a prudent management of institutional funds standard; and
to repeal certain provisions of  the  not-for-profit  corporation  law
relating thereto

PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL: This legislation will provide prudent
oversight  and  necessary  flexibility  for  charitable  endowments by
establishing  important  standards  to  govern  their  management  and
investment  through  the  enactment  in  New York State of the Uniform
Prudent Management of Institutional Funds Act (UPMIFA).

SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS: Section 1  of  the  bill  adds  a  new
Article 5-A to the Not-For-Profit Corporation law (Sections 550-558 as
outlined below):

Section 550: Short Title: The legislation creates the New York Prudent
Management  of  Institutional  Funds  Act based on a uniform model act
adopted in the majority  of  states  for  the  prudent  management  of
institutional endowment funds.

Section  551:  Definitions.  This section adds definitions for various
terms included in the new article: "Charitable  purposes,"  "Endowment
fund,"   "Gift   instrument,"   "Institution,"  "Institutional  fund,"
"Notice," "Person," "Program-related asset," and "Record."

Section  552:  Standard  of  conduct  in  managing  and  investing  an
institutional  fund.  This  section  provides  guidelines by which the
manager of institutional funds  must  manage,  invest,  and/or  retain
those  institutional  funds. This section also provides for duties for
the manager of the  institutional  funds  and  factors  that  must  be
considered when executing those duties.

Section   553:   Appropriation  for  expenditure  of  accumulation  of
endowment fund; rules  of  construction.  This  section  provides  the
factors  the  manager of institutional funds must consider when making
appropriations from or accumulation to the institutional funds.

Section 554: Delegation of management and investment  functions.  This
section  provides  for  the  rules  and  restrictions  under  which an
institution may delegate to  an  external  agent  the  management  and
investment   of  institutional  funds  and  provides  the  duties  and
obligations the agents accept upon delegation.

Section 555: Release or modification of  restrictions  on  management,
investment  or  purpose. This section provides that a court may modify
the charitable purpose or restrictions on institutional funds  due  to
impracticability,  unlawfulness,  impossibility,  or  wastefulness. It
would permit certain modifications upon notice to the Attorney General
for funds that are over 20 years old  and  are  valued  at  less  than
$250,000(such amount to be indexed to the CPI-U).

Section   556:   Reviewing  compliance.  This  section  provides  that
compliance with this Article shall not be viewed retrospectively.


Section 557: Application to existing institutional funds. This section
provides that this article shall apply to institutional funds existing
on or established after the effective date of this Article.

Section  558: Relation to Electronic Signatures in Global and National
Commerce Act. This section  provides  that  while  this  Article  does
modify,  limit, and supersede the Electronic Signatures and Global and
National Commerce Act, it does not modify, limit, or supersede Section
101 of that act or authorize the electronic delivery  of  any  notices
described in Section 103 of that Act.

Section  2  of  the  bill  repeals  selected  portions of Section 102,
Section 512, selected portions of Section 513, and Section 522 of  the
Not-For-Profit Corporation Law.

Sections  3  through 7 of the bill amend selected portions of Sections
406, 513, 514 and 717 of the Not-For-Profit Corporation Law to  comply
with this Article.

Section  8 of this bill amends selected portions of Section 2-b of the
Religious Corporations Law to conform to this Article.

Sections 9 through 12 of this bill amend selected portions of  Section
8-1.1,  Section  8-1.7  and Section 11-2.3 of the Estates, Powers, and
Trusts Law to ensure they do  not  conflict  with  the  Not-for-Profit
Corporation Law as added by this Article.

Section  13  of this bill amends Section 2115 of the Surrogate's Court
Procedure Act to conform to this Article

Section 14 of the bill amends paragraph 2  of  section  174-b  of  the
Executive Law to provide for notice to donors of changes to the law.

Section 15 of the bill contains a severability clause.

JUSTIFICATION:  As  a  result of the economic downturn and the reduced
value of investments, many non-profit organizations in New York  State
are  being  confronted  with  the  problem of "underwater endowments."
Under current New York law, these entities, which  include  charities,
colleges,   libraries,   museums,  foundations  and  other  non-profit
organizations, are prohibited from using portions of their  endowments
because  many  gifts  have decreased below their historic dollar value
(HDV), which is the value of the gifts on the date they were  received
by the endowment.

As  a  result,  many,  if  not  all,  of these organizations are being
prevented from utilizing their endowments at a time when they are most
needed. Since many non-profits are now  facing  budgetary  peril,  the
current  law  will  prevent hundreds of millions of dollars from being
spent for operating support, scholarships, research and a  vast  range
of  educational  and  charitable  purposes.  Further, preventing these
important organizations from spending to meet the intended purposes of
the donations can result in program cuts and layoffs in a sector  that
not only provides important services to the citizens of our state, but
is also a crucial part of New York's economy.


New  York  State  currently  follows  the  Uniform  Management  of the
Institutional Funds Act (UMIFA), drafted more than 35  years  ago  and
enacted  in New York in 1978. This new legislation, titled the Uniform
Prudent Management of Institutional Funds Act, or UPMIFA, updates  the
original  law  and has been adopted in more than 30 states since 2007,
even before the economic  downturn.  It  would  provide  guidance  and
authority  to  New  York's  charitable  organizations  concerning  the
management and investment of funds held by  those  organizations,  and
impose  additional  duties  on  those who manage and invest charitable
funds.

It would also resolve the problem of underwater endowments by removing
the focus on the HDV  and  placing  it  on  seven  prudent  investment
criteria.  It would allow non-profits to utilize their endowment funds
in furtherance of their created purpose,  while  protecting  both  the
assets and donors' intent, and readily assist cash-strapped charitable
organizations  at  no cost to the state. Additionally, re-codification
of these many disparate statutes would assist charitable organizations
and others in locating and following the law and bring  New  York  law
into conformity with other states.

PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY: None.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:  None.

EFFECTIVE DATE: September 1st
